hook.question_in_my_head: Why would one admiral with 13 ships take on 133, and how does he possibly survive or win?
hook.why: Strong David-vs-Goliath setup with a concrete number mismatch and a hint that even his own people think he's crazy. Slight confusion over 'ordered to give up the navy', but it adds intrigue.

who.Admiral Yi: Korean admiral who wants to keep fighting at sea with his last 13 ships instead of giving up the navy.
who.Yi's captains: Think he is crazy; they are afraid and hang back, leaving him to fight nearly alone.
who.The king: Wants Yi to give up the navy and fight on land; believes Yi has no navy left.
who.Japanese invasion fleet: Wants to destroy Yi and push through the strait with 133 ships.
who.The locals: Named the strait 'the crying strait' because of the roar of its water.

what_happened: Korea's navy was wiped out by a Japanese invasion fleet.
The king ordered Yi to give up the navy and fight on land.
Yi refused, saying he still had ships.
Yi anchored his 13 ships at the mouth of a narrow strait off Jindo island.
The Japanese fleet of 133 ships rushed in with the current behind them.
Yi's captains hung back, so his flagship fought almost alone.
The roaring of the water stopped, as the current turned.
The current reversed and pushed the Japanese ships backwards into each other.
Thirty-one Japanese ships were lost and none of Yi's.
why: The strait's current flips direction four times a day. The Japanese rode it in and got squeezed into a narrow gap where only a few ships could attack at once. When the tide turned, the same current that carried them in pushed them backward into one another, so Yi's few ships beat a much bigger fleet by using the water.
twist: The king thought Yi had no navy, but Yi's real weapon was the sea itself, whose current switches sides.
